about.title: Antioch Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A fall rarely announces itself. One moment you are walking into a grocery store off Lone Tree Way or crossing an apartment courtyard, and the next you are on the ground with a wrist that will not bear weight. In Antioch, a city of roughly 110,542 people in Contra Costa County, these injuries happen in ordinary places: parking lots along Hillcrest Avenue, stairwells, restaurant entryways, rental units where a landlord put off a repair. California premises liability law asks a specific question — did the owner know, or should the owner have known, about the hazard and then fail to fix it or warn you? That issue of notice is where most claims are decided, and it turns on evidence that vanishes quickly: a wet floor gets mopped, a broken step gets patched, surveillance footage gets overwritten within days. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect Antioch residents with an independent attorney who takes premises cases on contingency, meaning no fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Antioch Residents Use LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice is the whole case, and we know it
items.desc: California requires proof that the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The attorneys we connect you with focus early on inspection logs, maintenance records, and prior complaints that show what the property owner actually knew.

items.title: Video and photos are preserved before they disappear
items.desc: Most stores and apartment buildings overwrite surveillance footage in a matter of days. A prompt preservation letter, along with your own photos of the hazard, can be the difference between a supported claim and a disputed one.

items.title: Deadlines and shared fault are handled correctly
items.desc: You generally have two years to file, but a claim against a city or other public entity moves on a much shorter clock. California's pure comparative fault rule also means partial blame reduces, rather than erases, your recovery, and an attorney can push back on efforts to overstate your share.

items.question: I slipped on a wet floor in a store on Lone Tree Way and there was no sign. Do I have a claim?
items.answer: Possibly, but the missing sign alone is not enough. The key question is whether the store knew or should have known the floor was wet — for example, how long the spill sat there and whether employees had walked past it. Photos of the spill, the names of any witnesses, and a request that the store save its camera footage all help answer that question.

items.question: What if I tripped on a broken sidewalk or fell at a park owned by the City of Antioch?
items.answer: Claims against a public entity in California follow different rules than claims against a private business. You typically must file a formal government claim first, and the window for doing so is generally six months rather than two years. Because that deadline arrives quickly, it is worth talking to an attorney soon after a fall on public property.

items.question: The property owner says I was looking at my phone when I fell. Does that end my case?
items.answer: No. California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you are found partly responsible, you can still recover the portion of your damages attributed to the owner. The owner's insurer will often try to assign you a large share of the blame, which is one reason documenting the hazard itself matters so much.
